utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness another document, which is a letter of discharge from the hospital to the name of Mr. Sidik Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, we have not yet given a number to this last document that you made use of before showing the witness P-whatever. Anyway, the document which is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D860 consists of two pages, one B/C/S with ERN 70632892 and one which purports to be the English translation thereof with a different ERN number, that is 00650936.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, I hope you have this document before you, which says, "Sidik Ademovic, 1962, operated due to acute infection of pancreas and calculus gall bladder on the 7th of May 1993," and in connection with this, I will ask you the following: You were operated on in the hospital in Srebrenica which was in a very difficult situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell Their Honours for how long you were unable to move around or work after this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two months, and after that, I suffered serious consequences and the UNPROFOR representatives in the UN who had their offices in Potocari made it possible for me to be examined very often.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you another document now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before that, can we have an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document will become Exhibit D861. It consists of two pages, one in B/C/S and one in English. There doesn't seem to be an ERN number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at document D756 now. This is a list of war criminals known to the command of the 1st LPBR who perpetrated war crimes in Srebrenica, Bratunac, Milici, Vlasenica, and Skelani, and there are indicia that they are in Srebrenica, and it says below that "officials and organisers." Mr. Ademovic, please take a look at this list and you will see where it says commanders, your name, where it says -- it's on the third page in Bosnian,?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honours, on page 2 of the English translation, it's under number 74.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, I want to ask you: Have you ever committed a war crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll proceed. Now please look at page 1. Can you look at page 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the name under number 11, Dr. Sabit Begic. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Dr. Sabit is a very well respected citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the town of Srebrenica, and he spent the whole of the war in Sarajevo, from the 17th of April 1992, when he left Bratunac, at 1550 hours after the talks.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the name under number 23, Murat Efendic. Did he spend time in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. For three years before the war, he was in Sarajevo, and he spend the whole war there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under number 26, Besim Ibisevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just like Dr. Sabit at 1550 on the 17th of April 1992 after the meeting of Bratunac he left the area and he spent the entire period outside Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at number 70 and then 51 -- and then 51. Mr. Ismet Dautbasic, number 17, was a Professor and dean of the faculty of law in Sarajevo and he's not from Bratunac as it says here. He's from Brezovica and this man spent not more than 24 hours in Srebrenica over years and years. And this other person, Rizo Salmanagic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an eminent lawyer and he had spent very little time in Srebrenica and he had nothing to do with Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at Adil Osmanovic, Konjevic Polje, number 42.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was known as Theron [phoen]. This person spent some time in Tuzla after the outbreak of the war. After that he spent the entire period in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document then contain correct information and can these people be considered organisers, perpetrators, war criminals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This is a pure fabrication, pure forgery from this institute in bell grey, headed unfortunately by Mr. Ivanisevic. I apologise to Their Honours, but Mr. -- and the gentleman here and ladies, but Mr. Ivanisevic who invented these lists put me on one of these lists saying that I was an executioner in Jezestica on the 8th of August in his book about the chronicle of our graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now show the witness Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. P480?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 458, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 03593125 and page 03593126. These are pages 2 and 3 of this long document. Look here. It says "list of people in the Srebrenica municipality who are not assigned anywhere." Did you know the population of Jaglici well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know all the people living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the numbers 6 and 34. Six, Senahid Gusic, Jaglici. And then Osman Gusic, Jaglici, 34?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you, in the Srebrenica and Bratunac area, is there another place called Jaglici close to Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Neither in Srebrenica municipality nor in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These two persons here, Osman and Senahid Gusic, were they ever residents of Jaglici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please look at the next page and you will see under number 42, but let me ask you first, did you know all the inhabitants of your village of Susnjari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was born there and I still live there.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was there ever a person called Zijad Lilic living there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is there another place called Susnjari in the Srebrenica or Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. In the Krajina, near Banja Luka, there is a small village called Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Podrinje area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As I said, only as far as I recall in the area of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now put just a few brief questions to you. Do you remember in connection with some documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, which the OTP disclosed intending to use them -- I won't be able to discuss this now. It has to do with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'll ask you a general question first. While you were in Susnjari were you nominated as a member of some sort of Srebrenica assembly on behalf of Potocari during 1994, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I've heard of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In October 1994, did you attend some sort of meeting in the Srebrenica area or the Susnjari area or anywhere in your area at which there was discussion of a letter by the army commander General Rasim Delic addressed to Colonel Tihomir Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is the first time I've heard this. What has Tihomir Blaskic got to do with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to Their Honours who Tihomir Blaskic is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of that gentleman in early 2000 or 2002. Unfortunately, through this institution here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was he a commander of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, in central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the man. That's the man I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Srebrenica area, did you ever discuss such topics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no need. There would be no logic in it. Why would it have anything to do with our area?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Ademovic, look at me, please. Do you have a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may make a suggestion, may I address ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I'm asking you whether you have a problem. Because if you have a problem we need to solve it for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was one question, with all due respect to all of you, there was a misunderstanding. The question concerned Kravica. For your sake, for the sake of the Prosecution and the Defence, if I can say that I will be very grateful to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, please. You have a duty actually if there is a misunderstanding somewhere or you think that part of your testimony was not reported accurately, then you have a duty to point that out to us and rectify it. Go ahead. Take your time, as much time as you require.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's about something very important, an issue which will probably be important to everyone concerned. I understood the question, when asked by Madam Vidovic as to whether I entered Kravica, and I replied "no." I replied no because I had things in my hands and I didn't understand the context of the question properly. I think that Madam Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the witness said before that that he entered Kajici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said I hadn't entered Kravica. I was in Kajici, not Kravica. That is the context. So I did enter Kravica after 1200 hours, and I feel the need to tell you all this.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I put a question to clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is Kajici a part of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness replied that he entered the hamlet of Kajici and not Kravica proper, the centre of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So witness you did not enter Kravica proper, the centre of Kravica, but you did enter Kajici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Kajici, not yet in Kravica. I hadn't entered Kravica yet because there was shelling, there were people wounded, and this made it hard for me to move. That was the context, and I failed to express myself clearly to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you satisfied that you have explained it well now? Or do you want to give us further information or explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When asked by Madam Vidovic, if possible, she can put any other questions to me if she feels it necessary as to what I saw and experienced. I think it will be useful to everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, do you want to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. No, Your Honour, because I tried to avoid repeating testimony supplied by several previous witnesses. So I tried to abbreviate this testimony. I think the essence has been stated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Thank you, Mr. Ademovic. Mr. Di Fazio is now going to start his cross-examination. Your obligation pursuant to the solemn declaration that you made when you first started giving evidence, Mr. Ademovic, is to answer Mr. Di Fazio's question truthfully in accordance with your undertaking. May I also suggest now that more or less we know exactly how much time we have left until the end of business tomorrow, that you keep for the back of your mind the time left and you try to restrict your answers to what is necessary, without volunteering more details, unless of course you want to give explanations. Otherwise, you will be here over the weekend and we will have to continue with you on Monday, even though Mr. Di Fazio himself will be doing his utmost.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, well, I will, Your Honours. But can we revisit this matter just prior to breaking up for the day today, this issue of scheduling and timing and so on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If that's okay with the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. And if you think here and now that you require more time after the end of business tomorrow, then tell us so and we will-- I told you we make a distinction between one witness and another obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand that and I'm grateful, Your Honours. I fear we might have got to the point where I can't see wrapping up this witness, especially with the Defence who need time for their re-examination and any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not a problem. Ms. Vidovic took, I would imagine, more than seven hours, and I will not deprive you of any time which is not unreasonable anyway. Because if it does become unreasonable then we stop you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Madam Registrar, I think at this point you better alert the victims and witnesses office and, towards the end of today's sitting, then I will explain to the witness, all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic as you heard my name is Di Fazio. I'm one of the prosecutors here and I have some questions for you. And I endorse what everyone said to you. If you can keep your answers brief that will help you and me. Did you go to school in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you go to school with Mr. Oric, Naser Oric, in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't. I -- I'm his senior.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. So you're his senior?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this witness was born in '62 the other one was born in '67. There is five years' difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So -- thank you. Did you know him at school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really. We were children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what about in your later life, as an early adult? Did you know him then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I take it your answer is no. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you and what about in Srebrenica in late 1989, 1990, 1991. Did you know or meet Mr. Oric again around that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We used to come across each other but I did not know him as a person really. I did not know anything about his personality or character.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do I take it from your answer that you formed no particular relationship other than the fact that you were mere acquaintances? Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were acquaintances, but I had many acquaintances with whom I was much closer than with Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure. Did you ever become aware of Mr. Oric going to Belgrade, working in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of that, and that is why I told you that I grew up in one part of the world and he in the other, and we didn't know each other very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know what he did in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the earliest information I received, I knew that he was in security, on the police force, and later on he provided security for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And when did you first hear that and from whom? Or how did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard it from my colleagues, police officers in the Srebrenica police station. Mr. Oric would periodically come to the area in his spare time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. So I think you were a policeman from about 1981 up until about 1989 when you enrolled in the faculty of political science; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And it was during this particular time that you were a policeman based in the Srebrenica area that you saw Mr. Oric from time to time on his return from Belgrade and it was then that you learned of his activities in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you become aware of his working in any other area apart from Belgrade? For example, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was following this from the media. Because of the security situation in that region in the former Yugoslavia, it was there for everyone to see, not just me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure you were following it. But my question actually is: Did you become aware, did you ever become aware, of Mr. Naser Oric working in Kosovo for security forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know that he was part of the security forces for Mr. Milosevic. Now, where he was assigned, there must have been his superiors who were privy to that, and I did not really have occasion to find out about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wish to correct the interpretation. The witness stated that I knew that he worked for Milosevic providing security, but not in the security forces, which is totally different sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do I take it that you have no knowledge of any activities undertaken by Mr. Oric in Kosovo? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What his activities were and under whose orders, how would I know that? I was in Srebrenica and he was in Belgrade doing his job. It would be quite improper for me to say things before this Trial Chamber that are not then to be untrue. That would mean that I would be lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you to lie. On the contrary. On the contrary. So please don't -- just relax about that and you just tell us the truth. You -- okay. You met -- you said in evidence yesterday that you met Mr. Oric in April of 1992, in fact you said around the 20th of April 1992. And you were talking about uniforms at the time. I want to ask you about that meeting. First of all, where was the meeting? I'm not suggesting it was a formal meeting. An encounter. We will call it an encounter. Where was the encounter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was at Livade, in passing, in the village, just as everybody else that came across each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. And was Mr. Oric there in company with other men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the company of several lads, five or six of them, and there were always civilians there, women, children, and elderly, refugees who had started arriving by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But just to clarify so that you understand me, I'm not talking about refugees and civilians and the general population of the village. I'm talking about Mr. Oric. Now, who was in company with Mr. Oric, with Mr. Naser Oric, on this occasion on the 20th of April? Can you give us some details? You've said lads. What sort of lads? Can you remember how many lads, where they were from, remember their names, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said about the 20th of April, which doesn't necessarily mean that it was on the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. Perhaps not on the 20th. Around the 20th. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who were the lads with him? They were his acquaintances. I met these lads for the first time and if you're referring to their uniforms, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. saw this uniform -- these uniforms on the -- for the first time after the 11th of April 1992, after I left Srebrenica, and this remained impressed in my memory.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, after the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just to be absolutely clear, can you give us any idea of the numbers of men who were in company with Mr. Oric at this time? I'm still not entirely clear. Is it a question of ten or 20 or 30 or four or five men? I know -- and I know there has been a long time has passed since then but try and give us an idea of the size of the group in company with Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around the 20th, the first time I met them, there were around five or six of them. Later on probably the numbers increased. I heard there were some 10 or 15 men and the number varied from -- at different periods. I believe that there may have been at most 15 to 20 men. But at the time that I saw them, there were five or six of them and I cannot tell you anything else because I would be making things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure, sure. And this is the occasion when you discovered that they had acquired the uniforms, Mr. Naser Oric and the group of men, the five or six men who were with him, they had acquired their uniforms from Arkan's men by setting up an ambush in Potocari. Is that -- that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Arkan was well known back then, wasn't he, in 1992? He was a notorious figure, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Famous throughout the former Yugoslavia, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And everybody knows why.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. Quite right. And so for Mr. Oric and his associates to have ambushed Arkan and taken the uniforms from them, was a very considerable feat of bravery, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just that the evidence is it was Arkan's men, not that it was actually Arkan himself. I think that needs to be made clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It was Arkan's men. Arkan and his men were notorious throughout the former Yugoslavia, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And I've already said that one knows why they were famous and it was with these intentions that they came to the areas of Bratunac and Srebrenica. I believe everybody was quite clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure. And for Mr. Oric and his associates to have dealt with these Arkan's men was a feat of quite some bravery, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, yes. And if I may continue? If the Arkan's men entered Srebrenica, torched and killed, scorched and raped many inhabitants of Srebrenica, was it not then courage to stand ground and oppose such villains at the time? Had I been there I would have done the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right with respect, aren't you? It was -- it was something that had to be done and Mr. Oric and his associates had performed a feat that was going to become well known in the Srebrenica area. Am I correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And he was thought to be a very brave man. After that, he -- I always considered him a courageous and honest man. Had I been there I would have participated in the ambush after all the crimes that the Arkan's men had committed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And this feat in ambushing Arkan's men, these tough fellows, became well known throughout the Srebrenica area and made Mr. Oric a popular, well-known figure in the area, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But only by his courage, by nothing else. For the rest he was just a citizen, just as I was. In some other areas of life I enjoyed more respect than Oric. It was only in this respect and for these reasons that he was respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But given the situation that was developing in your area, in your particular area, and in the Srebrenica area, this feat in ambushing Arkan's men, presumably wounding or killing them to the point where he was able to secure uniforms, was something that made him respected and brought fame to him, isn't it? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was respected only for his courage but not for anything else. I repeat: I enjoyed more respect as a citizen in some other walks of life in Srebrenica than him, and I speak upon full responsibility. I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. How did -- can you recall how it came up in conversation that the ambush had occurred and that Arkan's men had been -- had had their uniforms taken off them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question, how it came up.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, on the 20th or -- sorry, around the 20th of April 1992, Mr. Naser Oric turns up at this location that you've mentioned and he's got five or six men who are dressed in camouflage uniforms which you find out were taken, retrieved, from Arkan's men. Okay? How did that topic come up in conversation? How did you find out about it? That's all I want to know. On this day around the 20th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was because I heard the shooting, and because the people talked about it. The people were moving from Potocari to my village all the way up to the 2nd of May. At that time, I myself descended to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And what were the people saying about this episode where Arkan's men had been ambushed? What were they saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The stories varied of course because the people talk. I went down into the area to see for myself what had really happened. Of course, different men tell different stories, and one always prefers to see things with one's own eyes before believing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure. And so I take it that it was -- that the whole episode had already acquired a notoriety? I don't mean that in any bad sense but the whole episode was already famous and well known. Different groups of people were talking about it. You actually went down to see the site where this ambush had occurred, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was on that day and all the way through to the demilitarisation, or rather after the 10th of August 1992, that I did not have an opportunity to meet the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there is a mix-up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, you put -- repeat the question, please, and the important thing is that we make sure that it is being interpreted well or at least that he understands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll try and make it simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can, yes, please. I don't think it was complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The episode with Arkan, the ambush that Mr. Oric and his -- sorry, with Arkan's men, that Mr. Oric and his men had participated in was quite well known throughout the Muslim community. Different groups, different people were already talking about it, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This raised our spirits and our morale for all of us. It made us stronger. It made us believe that one can oppose even the Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That not even they were impossible to conquer, and invincible, and that even they could be stopped from further bloodshed, massacre, and intimidation. I don't think we should dwell much on the Arkan's men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I might just dwell on it a little bit longer, if that's all right. When you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you say that it raised our spirits and our morale, you're talking, aren't you, about the Muslim people in the wider Srebrenica area, not just talking about your village, your more -- the area just around Susnjari. You're talking about the wider area around Srebrenica, aren't you? That's where spirits were raised and morale was raised amongst the Muslim people, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only speak for Potocari and my area. I cannot speak for the rest. This is a very wide area, some 40 or 60 kilometres. I was unable to know what was going on over there, what their morale was, what the people were talking. I can speak for my environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it would be necessary for me to speak about the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: From everything that you heard and saw and observed in 1992, 93, 94, and 95, would you agree with me that Mr. Naser Oric was a brave and courageous soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was as brave a soldier as I was and all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the leaders of a group of some 15 to 20 men, just as I was the leader of my 25 men, and Naser Oric had a group of some 15 to 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would you say that you were as well known throughout the Srebrenica area, amongst the Muslim population, Bosniak population, as you -- as he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my village of Susnjari, I was a respected man, as well as in the neighbouring villages of Jaglici and Brezova Njiva. I was a respected, honest man then, just as I believe I am today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not -- honestly, I'm not suggesting anything about your respectability or your honesty. I'm just asking you a very simple question. Would you say you were as well known throughout the Srebrenica area amongst the Muslim population as Mr. Oric was? If you can comment on that, please let us know. If you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The citizens of Srebrenica, all of them, including Serbs, Muslims and Croats, knew me as a policeman and trusted me because I discharged my duties in a professional manner and with full responsibility, without making any distinctions on any basis. As for my own village of Susnjari and the neighbouring villages of Jaglici and Brezova Njiva, naturally the people liked me, just as they did in some other places, but, of course, my village had a special place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll try and approach it this way. Was Mr. Naser Oric well known in the Srebrenica area in 1992 and 1993? Was he famous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only by what he had done in Potocari. For the rest, there were better, more diligent and honest men. To the best of my knowledge. Perhaps in his group, yes. I myself respected him for that particular segment. As for the other matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever hear the Serbs speaking about him when you were listening to what they had to say over the radio? Serb forces, I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They used to mention him and his group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname, Mr. Naser Oric? A nickname? Did Mr. Naser Oric have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. To the extent I know, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, let's move on from Mr. Oric and let's talk about your group. You gave evidence that there were some groups that were formed in the Susnjari area and you recall you said there was a group formed in your village. You were the leader. And just to be clear, there were groups also formed in Jaglici and a place called Brezova Njiva; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, groups. There was a group in Jaglici and a group in Brezova Njiva.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness can be shown the map very briefly. It's D841. It's the big one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic I've had trouble finding Brezova Njiva. I wonder if you can point it out to me. I had no problems with Jaglici and Susnjari. But Brezova Njiva what I would like to you find for me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness did mark it on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. My recollection is that he did. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Look, I'm sorry, I didn't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is marked on my map, for example. It's marked by 2 letters, B and N. The problem is --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, is it just slightly to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can show you where I marked it but I have to find my map first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I thought it was a different spelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I marked it for my own uses, obviously. It is between Jaglici and Susnjari and he pointed there at roughly equal distance between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can see now it's BN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I put BN there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I apologise to the Chamber. It went over my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. This gets complicated sometimes. You're not the only one who finds it difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And again, pardon my -- sorry, Ms. Usher, I don't need the map just for the moment. My apologies. And was there another group also formed in a village called or an area called Babalica or Babuljica, something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was established only later, later. I said it had 15 men and its leader was Mensur Misanovic [phoen]. I think I said quite enough about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I think again there is a misunderstanding. You're asking about a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think he is answering about a village. He is answering about a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Look, I'll try and deal with it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've given history -- you've given testimony about the formation of your group in Susnjari, in Jaglici, Brezova Njiva, and now I'm asking about a fourth place, a fourth location, something like Babalica or Babuljica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is a village. It is a village quite far from me. To the south of my area. But initially, the people had moved out of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Let's concentrate on the three villages --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- excuse me. You can see if you look at the map. I apologise. If you look at the map, you can see in the map that it's not in my area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. We will concentrate on the villages in your area, okay? Now, were they all formed at about the same time, these groups that you've been speaking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At various intervals of time. I put myself at the disposal on the 18th, which doesn't mean that the group was actually formed on the 18th, because I said in my testimony that we already had problems around recognising people's status and membership, because of these groups, because they wouldn't accept us as such, as legal members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We had to prove in an administrative procedure, retroactively where we had belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't know if I'm not making myself clear and I apologise to you if I'm not. I'm not asking you about the legal niceties of whether or not you were or were not a member of the ABiH Army. What I'm asking you is this: Were the groups that you talked about, the independent local groups, in Susnjari, Jaglici, in Brezova Njiva, were they all formed at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. around the same time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere in the first 10 days after the 18th of April, and up to the end of April, in that space of time. It was all spontaneous. It wasn't well organised. People were still leaving Srebrenica and Bratunac, going off towards Tuzla or other European countries. There was still a lot of confusion, a lot of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Fine. As far as your particular group was concerned, the Susnjari grouping, at the beginning, when it was first formed, you had about 20 rifles and some pistols, thereabouts, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said that. Some 20 weapons, either rifles or pistols, but I do have to point out, as I said, that these were weapons for which people had licences. They were hunting rifles and this includes pistols or carbines. I had my official automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I heard all your evidence, thank you, yesterday and the day before. Thank you. That's fine. Did your group acquire more weapons throughout 1992? Now, I know that you said in evidence in late June you got a few more. But I'm talking about the whole year. Did your Susnjari group acquire more weaponry as the year wore on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In the way I described during conflicts, clashes. Let me just mention one detail. On the 29th of June, the 29th of June, at Hajducko Groblje when we set an ambush -- or, rather, when an ambush was set for the refugees going off, we captured some weapons and a combat kit and some infantry weapons and we exchanged these so that we replenished our weapons, our store of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a question of the transcript. The witness said when -- that they got the weapons, when an ambush was set for the refugees, whereas here it says when they set an ambush for the refugees, which is quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sure that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All I want to know is this: As the year wore on and you approached the end of the year 1992 what sort of numbers of weaponry did your group have and what type of weapons did your group have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had mixed, a mixed assortment or weapons, hunting rifles, carbines, still all with licences. Then there were the automatic weapons we captured, in the way I described, when we were ambushed by Serb forces in various places and during the fighting, when we were attacked, and then we would wait until we were sure and they would throw their weapons away and we would collect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I heard all of that. That's not a problem, okay? My question is this: By the end of the year, what had you acquired? Just that. What did you have? Dutch one Zolja, 15 Zoljas, 35 automatic weapons, grenades? Just tell us -- give us a brief summary of what your group had by way of weaponry by the end of the year. That's all I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything I've enumerated so far. I had this and after the 6th of August, the big ambush and massacre at Hajducko Groblje, another M53, and approximately, because I can't recall the exact number, several semi-automatic rifles. That was all. As for Zoljas and what you're talking about, I knew nothing of that because it was the other side firing from those weapons in my area where people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you for answering my question. Now what about membership of your group? By the end of the year what sort of numbers did your group have? And I know you told us that it fluctuated from time to time, but at the end of 1992, how big was it, the Susnjari group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had 25, sometimes the number would increase for various reasons. Sometimes people would leave because this was not obligatory so they would leave to look for ford for their families so that you would come to the position where you left him and he would be gone. More or less --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You would agree with me on -- sorry, let me withdraw that and rephrase it. Am I correct that there was really no significant improvement in the weaponry held by your group or the numbers of men, fighters, in your group from the time you started out by the end of 1992? A few more extra automatic weapons and that's about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said several automatic rifles and, in the course of 1992, two M53s but we took this in two different ways. One was on the 29th of June and the other on the 6th of August and the little on the 8th of August but that was very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you had the same shortage of weaponry throughout all of 1992? You could never substantially improve your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how. We were only helped in a certain time period depending on the situation and the attack by the group from Jaglici or the group from Brezova Njiva, if in their areas there were not intense infantry attacks. And if they came to our assistance, they got weapons or ammunition in the same way. And that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. But apart from the scavenging of odd weapons following military encounters, you didn't actually acquire much in the way of weaponry or fighters throughout 1992, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The amounts the Serbs had, we didn't have. But we had enough to wait because every bullet was worth its weight in gold. Every bullet could mean a life. So we didn't waste any. We didn't have bread to eat, let alone ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your capacity to resist the Serbs and their technological -- and their technological advantage that they had didn't change substantially, did it, from April 1992 to December 1992, on your evidence? Would you agree with that proposition; no significant difference, a few extra automatic weapons, that's all you got, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct as far as my group goes. I did have another advantage because our geographical position, location, gave me a greater chance with far less equipment and, by making sure that no bullet was wasted, to survive. Otherwise we would have suffered a disaster like the one in 1995. I have to say that there were two other groups in the area who would occasionally come to my assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I was going to ask you about those other two groups, the Jaglici and the Brezova Njiva group, okay? Did their position vis-a-vis weaponry and fighters remain basically static throughout 1992, as yours had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The situation was the same as in my case. The numbers increased somewhat but not a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now we will move on to another aspect of these groups that I'd like to know about. Firstly, can you briefly tell us how it came to be that you were made leader of your group? Briefly, please, Mr. Ademovic. I just want to know how it happened. Was it a meeting, an election, discussion? Just tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no meeting. There was no election, if you mean a legal procedure, systematic and chronological process. It was all spontaneous on the part of the local villagers in the village because they saw what was going on from Croatia and further afield. I was hesitant to accept, and had not the situation been what it was, I would never have accepted. But with hindsight I would do the same again. I would not, however, wish my experiences on my worst enemy. I wouldn't want my worst enemy to be put in the same situation that I was in. You can imagine what I knew, what I'd seen, and when you're desperate --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, I'm very fortunate not to have had your experiences. All I'm asking you is a very simple question, okay? How did you become leader? That's all. How did it happen? I'm not asking for -- I'm not suggesting you should have followed any procedure or that you wrested power from someone. I'm just asking you: How did you become leader? That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically if I could assist here, intervene. What Mr. Di Fazio want to know is how come that out of all the people in Susnjari -- in your village, the choice fell on you and not on someone else? This is what we want to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll put it simply. I arrived in my village through the woods. I brought an official automatic rifle with me. And they saw their entire security hanging on that one single automatic rifle at the time. I would have been happy had someone else taken it or had there been more such weapons, unfortunately. But I happened to have this weapon. And people saw their security as hanging on that single rifle. And although I did so reluctantly, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Well, what sort of control did you exert over this group in the months that followed your becoming leader of the group? In particular, what I want to know is this: Were you able to tell the men where to go and fight, how to -- first that question. Were you able to tell them where to go and where to fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for control and issuing orders, it was all voluntary. There was a patriotic commitment, but I couldn't issue an ultimatum to someone or say to them, "You have to go there. You have to do this." I want to clarify this. I do apologise, but I have said in my testimony that it was not an obligation. People would leave. They did leave. People from my group left to look for food because the situation was what it was, for various reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So if you had planned an action to take place in two or three or four days' time that required ten men, at any point of time in the next two or three or four days, any number of those ten men could have come and said to you, "No, I'm sorry, I'm not going to go and participate in that action." That was always a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, sir. With all due respect, what could we have planned? Does it say anywhere we planned anything? All the time we just waited. We didn't go anywhere. There was no planning. What kind of planning? I was only in my own area with these men with the capacities we had. The manpower I had, the -- and the gun I had --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The rifle, that is, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- the MTS. All I could do was make use of the configuration of the terrain in order to save myself and others. All I wanted was to avoid being hit by a bullet and being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But you've given us extensive evidence of being involved in -- well, yes, of being involved in military encounters at the very least. And when you were involved in these military encounters, you were doing so with members of your own group, weren't you, Kravica, and places like that? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. With the groups who came to me under the circumstances that prevailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were involved in these military activities with members of your group, did you ever think in advance about what you were going to do? Did you plan it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have any opportunity to plan anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only thing that happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, please. Let me describe it specifically. When I set out towards Kravica, I didn't plan anything. The only thing I could plan was looking for bread and perhaps a bullet or two, because, as I said, I was hungry and I ate grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So is it that your testimony to the Trial Chamber, that from April of 1992 until demilitarisation, you and your group made no plan for any military activity at all? Is it -- do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My whole testimony, if you followed it, you and the esteemed gentlemen, described my own area, the struggle to survive, to survive, to stay alive, and to help the refugees, of whom there were enormous numbers there, to help them somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, I'm not asking you about the suffering of your people, okay? I'm not. I'm asking you about military activity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. I, as far as military activities, or plans to attack, I had none of that. There was no possibility of that. And everything I've said so far goes to confirm this. There was only the struggle to survive. You can imagine planning an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You made no plans for any attacks. What about plans for defending your village? Did you make any plans for defending Susnjari using this group of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please. If you're being attacked, with that kind of force, would you defend your own house? Under the circumstances I was in, I was born there, I was not attacking anyone. I had what I had. And what I had, and they were slaughtering and killing people, and people wanted bread. They had nothing to eat. What would you have done in my situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not criticising you, Mr. Ademovic. I can fully understand that you would want to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise. I do have feelings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. I'm not seeking to mislead you or to upset you in any way. All I want to know is about planning and how your group operated. I want to know how they worked, how they functioned, okay? So did you make any plans for the defence of your village? Because you had good reason to, okay? So did you make any plans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If in one day on Ravni Buljim and Rupoglav in that tiny area, there would be 3.000 projectiles of various calibres falling, landing in that area. What would you have done in that situation? Would you have climbed the tree or dug a dugout?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have got five minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have eight minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Eight minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think I've reached the end of this particular topic for the moment, if Your Honours please, and I'd like to consider what I -- my position as far as cross-examination goes. I may be able to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not -- certainly not making any promises but I might be able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But -- I do appreciate what you're saying and I think -- I know exactly what you mean. However, you have to understand that we cannot operate in limbo as regards witnesses. I cannot leave today here and leave the witness not knowing whether he is going back on Saturday or whether he is going back on Monday or on Tuesday. As we are going, if you continue and finish your cross-examination, we will be here Tuesday if not Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's a fair assessment, believe me. I know what I am saying. But he has got a family, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And he needs to let his family know when he is going back. And I have, together with Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, and we have talked about this several times, a responsibility to minimise the costs of this Tribunal as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I find myself in a peculiar situation. Let me say this. If I proceed with the cross-examination that I have planned so far, and plan on working on tonight, there is no way that we will finish tomorrow. It's out of the question, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can quite understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I, however, just wish to tell the Trial Chamber that I may decide to at some point tomorrow cut it short. That's all I'm saying. As presently advised we are not going to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Registrar, I understand that the Victims and Witnesses Unit are monitoring the sitting so they follow what's going on. So I'm just tasking you with coordinating with them, explain to them if they have not understood what the situation is, and then they know which preparations to provide for or make. As far as you, Mr. Ademovic, the situation -- you've heard me. I wish I were in a position to tell you here and now tomorrow we'll finish and you can go home on Saturday. As it is, I don't know what the situation is. So I am informing the victims and witnesses unit, who are usually in charge of making arrangements for your return back home, that -- to leave options open. In other words, not to close the option of taking -- sending you back home on Saturday if Mr. Di Fazio brings his cross-examination to an end tomorrow. If not then we are obviously leer Monday, if not also Tuesday, and I don't know what days there are flights to wherever you wish to go because I don't know where you're living now and I don't want to know. So that's the position. Just wanted to put your mind at rest that we are taking an interest in trying to leave all options open so as not to leave you here unnecessarily. All right? So we will adjourn now. Tomorrow, as I said, Ms. Vidovic and Mr. Wubben, it's 9.00. Is it the same courtroom? It is still here in Courtroom I at 9.00 in the morning instead of quarter past 200. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of October, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.
